1) Commit smoothing / true-up cadence: Does Redwood offer quarterly true-ups (preferred) or is it strictly annual? If quarterly, how do you handle negative/positive variances and invoice credits?
2) Overage math: confirm whether overage is charged at a flat multiplier of the committed unit price or on a tiered basis. Any caps or protections?

Lisa — thanks for the clear list. Quick summary below; attaching the pricing termsheet and a commit schedule template for your finance team to model. Happy to hop on a short call if you prefer.

Executive summary (one page):
- Commit cadence: Quarterly true-ups (preferred) by default for deals of this size. Quarterly true-up reconciles actual consumption vs committed tokens; positive variance consumes committed balance first, negative variance -> surplus credit application up to cap (see below). Annual true-up is available on request.
- Anchored floor: We propose an anchored monthly floor equal to 70% of the annualized commit divided by 12 (min monthly bill). This protects capacity while allowing short-term usage variance.
- Overage: Tiered overage ladder applied to usage above the monthly committed allowance after any surge windows. Bands: up to 20% over commit billed at 1.25x unit rate, next 50% at 1.6x, remainder at 2.0x. (Rationale: progressive pricing discourages sustained surges while avoiding immediate punitive rates).
- Surplus credits: Unused committed tokens convert to surplus credits and are applied forward quarter-to-quarter up to 50% of the next quarter's commit. Surplus credits expire after 4 quarters.
- Surge protection: Rolling 2-month surge window per quarter where up to 20% additional consumption is billed at committed rate (no overage multiplier) to support product launches or batch jobs. Limit: 3 surge windows per rolling 12 months.
- Invoicing / true-up timing: Quarterly true-up invoice with line-item credits for surplus; credits reduce future invoices; any net payable is due per standard payment terms.

Attachments: Redwood_Pricing_Termsheet_v1.pdf (pdf - 110KB), MG_Commit_Schedule.xlsx (xls - 28KB)

If that aligns with OmniFin's expectations I'll loop Ben and our commercial team to propose minor variant options (e.g., larger anchored floor / expanded surge protection in exchange for increased commit).

Best,

Looping in a couple commercial levers we can offer for OmniFin that help differentiation without materially lowering unit economics:

1) Surge protection (alternate): Instead of 3 small windows, offer a 12-month rolling surge protection where the first 20% monthly overage (up to two consecutive months) given once per quarter is billed at the committed unit rate. This buys them launch flexibility; we can make it tradeable (unused surge bucket rolls forward but counts against surplus cap).
2) Overage ladder tweak: Make the first band (<=20%) 1.15x for strategic customers with a commitment uplift (e.g., +15% annual commit). This gives them a de facto cushion when they pay a little more for predictability.
3) Surplus credit expansion: Increase forward-crediting cap to 66% of next quarter's commit if they sign a 24-month term and agree to a mild annual CPI index (helpful for forecasting).
4) SLA credit: For enterprise SLAs we can include a billing credit (percentage of monthly invoice) tied to missed p50/p90 latency SLOs; works well as a negotiation sweetener.

Also — add internal note: ask legal to draft a short exhibit describing "surge protection mechanics" and a sample invoice showing one quarter with surplus credits and one with true overage. I'll attach a sample invoice once we settle language.
